chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all together, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Abdullah ibn Maymun al-Qaddah, from Abu Abdillah, from his father, from his forefathers (peace be upon them), who said:

There were two men in Medina, one called Hayt and the other Mani'. They said to a man, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was listening: 'When you go to Al-Taif, God willing, then take the daughter of Ghaylan al-Thaqafiyyah, for she is a candle, miserly, moist, slender, sweet. When she sits, she bends; when she speaks, she sings. She comes with four and goes back with eight, and between her legs is like the cup.'

So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'I do not view you two as being among the men devoid of physical desire.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ordered that they be exiled to a place called Al-Araya, and they would trade there every Friday.

key_terms.أُولِي الْإِرْبَةِ: Men devoid of physical desire / men of continence
key_terms.الْعَرَايَا: Al-Araya, a place of exile near Medina

ai.seo_question: What does the term 'ulī al-irbah' mean in the context of the Prophet's judgment of the two men?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) identifies two men, Hayt and Mani', as lacking 'ulī al-irbah' (men of physical desire or potency) after observing their detailed, appreciative commentary on a woman’s physical attributes in Al-Taif. This incident is often cited by Shia scholars to illustrate the concept of sexual potency and desire as a marker of masculine virility, with the men's exile to Al-Araya serving as a social consequence of their perceived deficiency.
